sources.title: Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition
sources.publisher: Journal of Consumer Research 32(1), Thomas & Morwitz
sources.notes: Experiments on how nine-ending prices are perceived; effect tied to a change in the leftmost digit.

sources.title: Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales: Evidence from Field Experiments
sources.publisher: Quantitative Marketing and Economics 1(1), Anderson & Simester
sources.notes: Mail-order catalog field experiments comparing $9-ending prices with nearby prices. Add the DOI after checking.

sources.title: Psychological pricing
sources.notes: Overview only; use to find primary sources, not as the sole support for a claim.

claims.text: People give disproportionate weight to the leftmost digit of a price (left-digit effect).
The effect appears mainly when the leftmost digit changes (e.g. 2.99 vs 3.00).
Catalog field experiments reported higher demand at some 9-ending prices than at slightly lower prices.
Nine endings are associated with discounts, so premium brands often prefer round prices.
